Weapons of mass surveillance - Journeyman Pictures

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Governments with dubious human rights records are now using mass surveillance technology to thoroughly track and quell any murmurs of dissent

Unique Selling Point:
The digital age has heralded a new unprecedented means of surveillance, and as more of our personal information goes online, more of our lives are subject to state-sponsored espionage. Governments with dubious human rights records are now using mass surveillance technology to thoroughly track and quell any murmurs of dissent - and it is western companies that are providing the technology to do so. BBC reporter Nawal al-Maghafi investigates

Script:


Visuals Story/Sync/Comm

1. Nawal Al Maghafi – Correspondent PTC






Blacked out FOIs



Imagery from ETI brochure (eye, jigsaw puzzle, access button, capabilities headings)


Arab Spring images (images are stripped of sound, slowed down)

British government/Saudi images.






















NAWAL PTC

This is a film about a world in which surveillance has no limits, and what can happen when it’s in the hands of repressive governments.

MANAL SYNC
It used to be that walls had ears. Now it’s smartphones have ears.

NAWAL PTC
This is the story of how British technology may have helped silence a generation in the Arab world.

MARIETJE SYNC
Each and every case where everyone is silenced or ends up in prison with the help of EU-made technologies I think is unacceptable.

NAWAL PTC
Our investigation shows how Britain’s leading weapons manufacturer has profited from exporting sophisticated, officially classified equipment.

NICK WEAVER SYNC
Every country willing to write a pay check to the right party can do this sort of surveillance but no one wants to admit it.

NAWAL PTC
We reveal that some of this equipment is so powerful, that foreign governments who’ve bought it have the capability of using it against the UK and its allies. Threatening national security.
2. TITLE

WEAPONS OF MASS SURVEILLANCE

3.



Daytime drone shots over Beirut

More sound effect with voices chattering

COMM

In this film we show that powerful British cyber surveillance equipment has secretly been sold to repressive governments in the Middle East.

Our investigation begins in Beirut, the Lebanese capital.

4.

PTC Nawal PTC

I’ve come to Beirut because we’ve tracked down an expert on cyber security expert from the region. He lives out of a suitcase because with so many people at risk, he’s constantly travelling to train people how to protect themselves.

5. Nawal with Maskati infecting phone









COMM

Mohammed Maskati works with human rights organisations, journalists and activists. He’s going to show me how easy it is for a government to get access to my phone.

MASKATI UPSOT
I’m installing the malware. It’ll give me full access to the device.

He’s infecting it with a spyware programme. This could also be done remotely, by a government; but it’s old school, off the shelf technology.
6. COMM

Today it’s possible to pin down someone’s location, read their emails, even change their text messages. And that’s just the beginning.

7. Aston

Mohammed Maskati
Digital Security Consultant MASKATI SYNC

I can activate the microphone to listen in, or take pictures with the phone. That’s why I cover up all cameras so no one can take pictures of meetings or places I go.

8.
Nawal in car, leaves Beirut


COMM

I’m leaving Lebanon to start my journey into the Gulf region. But even when I’m in another country, Mohammed will be able to see right into my life.

9. Maskati tracking Nawal’s phone


UPSOT MASKATI

At 7:00 she was at Dubai international airport. She changed the sim to a local one. We can see all the contacts Nawal stored in the phone. And all the messages she’s sent and received.

10. Big wide top shot Dubai

COMM

And Mohammed is right. I am in Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates.

11. Ahmed collecting kids.


COMM

I’ve come here to meet Ahmed Mansoor. He’s an activist who was imprisoned for tweeting about abuses by the UAE government.

It has spent so much money targeting him that he’s become known as the million-dollar dissident.

12. Aston

Ahmed Mansoor
AHMED MANSOOR SYNC

Being watched is a horrible feeling. You lose your freedom because you cannot move. It’s a violation of your privacy. It’s like having a stranger in your bedroom.

13.
Ahmed driving past prison

COMM

Ahmed was protesting against unfair trials and arbitrary detention. He was also charged with insulting the nation’s leadership.

14. Ahmed showing Nawal images on his phone

COMM

He shows me how his e-mail was hacked exposing all his messages and contacts.

15. AHMED SYNC

This is what is known as a phishing site. It looks like Google but it’s not. They ask you to enter your password. Then they clone it and have access to your email.

15a Citizen Lab Report

COMM

An independent investigator said that the UAE government was almost certainly responsible.

16. In car

COMM

Following his release from jail, Ahmed isolated himself to protect his friends and family.

18. AHMED SYNC

You leave home not knowing whether you’ll come back or not.

19.


COMM

I stayed in touch with Ahmed after we finished filming. But then, in March 2017, I heard he’d disappeared.

Weeks later his family discovered he was being held in solitary confinement without charge in al-Sadr prison in Abu Dhabi.

20.






COMM

According to the UAE news agency, his crime was using social media to spread:

‘false and misleading information that harms national unity and damages the country’s reputation.’

His case has caused alarm world-wide.


21. Aston

James Lynch,
Amnesty International
JAMES LYNCH SYNC

If you look at a context like the UAE where a human rights defender like Ahmed Mansoor has been punished simply for speaking out against the government in favour of human rights, then the implications of sending or providing sophisticated surveillance equipment to monitor communications of activists in civil society are very serious.

22. Ahmed at computer COMM

Ahmed was arrested because of his social media posts.

23. Graphic










COMM

But we’ve discovered that the UAE has the power to monitor his private communications too. In fact it has the power to monitor all of its people, all of the time.

It now has a kind of surveillance that doesn’t infect the phone or computer. It’s completely external and so it’s almost impossible to detect.

It’s called mass surveillance.

24. Maskati interview MASKATI SYNC

Mass surveillance is aimed at people in general, a community, people in an organisation.

25.
COMM

As in the West, governments in the Arab world have invested millions in mass surveillance. It’s a uniquely powerful tool for learning what the population is up to.

26.

MASKATI SYNC

Let’s say a new human rights group has emerged. The State doesn’t not know the specific individuals, so it might begin with mass surveillance, all members of the group are monitored. Information gathered from the mass surveillance can identify the key individuals. The focus can be narrowed down.

27. Nawal at Copenhagen airport COMM

This kind of mass surveillance has chilling implications for all of us.

What’s shocking is where it’s coming from – one of the world’s most liberal countries.

28. Top shot Aalborg, Denmark



COMM

This is Aalborg, in Denmark. A former industrial city reinventing itself as a centre for the new knowledge economy.

29. Bridge COMM

I’m heading over the bridge to a place called Norresundby.

30. Nawal driving



Statics of building COMM

I’m going to visit a company that specialises in cyber surveillance.

It was called ETI.

In 2011 it was bought by BAE, the UK’s biggest arms manufacturer. Today it’s called BAE Systems Applied Intelligence. And it makes a surveillance system that’s been sold to the United Arab Emirates.

31. Satellite dishes COMM

Around the back, two large satellite dishes. An employee wants to know what we’re doing.

32. Exchange with employee







UPSOT

EMPLOYEE
What’s the reason you’re filming?

Do you know who we make cyber-security for?

NAWAL
No. That’s what we want to know. Who do you make cyber-security for?

EMPLOYEE
That’s why we don’t answer you.

NAWAL
It seems very secretive, whatever it is.

EMPLOYEE
It’s a weapons manufacturer, and by that you will know that being a weapons manufacturer, they’re not going to say anything. So that’s the policy.

33. Final shot of ETI building
COMM

And nobody would speak to us.

34. ETI building




COMM

But after months of research, we found a former employee who agreed to talk about his former work, provided his identity was disguised. He is portrayed by an actor.

35. Anonymised interview of Jo. JO SYNC

You were always under some kind of surveillance. You weren’t sure who your friends were, who your enemies were.

There were different rooms you couldn’t go into if you didn’t have a specific level of clearance. After a while I was allowed to go into those rooms. That’s where they kept the equipment.

36.
Graphic COMM

This surveillance solution was so closely guarded because of its extraordinary power. It can
collect, catalogue and analyse millions of peoples communications, both private and public.

37. Jo anonymised interview









JO SYNC

You’d be able to intercept any internet traffic. If you wanted to do a whole country, go ahead. You’d probably need something to narrow your search down, either by a specific person, a specific email address, specific IP address or specific keywords to search for.

38. Graphics and brochure details




COMM

The surveillance tool goes by multiple names but one of them is ‘Evident’. It’s one of the reasons BAE wanted to buy the Danish cyber security company.

This sales brochure describes Evident as a highly sophisticated tool for mass surveillance that is able to integrate targeted capabilities too.

39. Jo interview JO SYNC

You could pinpoint peoples’ location based on cellular data. You could follow people around. They were quite far ahead with voice recognition. They were capable of decrypting stuff as well.

40. Studio pictures COMM

Governments have always collected information about us.
But we now generate much more data about ourselves,
And technological advances make it far easier for the state to collect it.


AD BREAK ONE


41.

Nawal stands in front of a screen with her phone in her hand. Camera moves past her into the graphic.

Data flows into an ISP, at first a trickle and then a stream.

The web becomes vast and intricate.

Cutaways of Nawal watching screen

NAWAL PTC

This is my not-so-secret device.
It’s sending out information about me every second of the day.

(Out of vis)

That information is called metadata.
It tells the internet service provider
my phone is the source of the message, along with dates, times, subject lines, locations -

(In vis)

- and numbers or addresses of the people I am communicating with.

43. Aston

Dr. Nicholas Weaver
University of California, Berkeley NICK WEAVER SYNC

(out of vis) All you do is basically record what people are doing and search it later.

(in vis) So, if I’m an intelligence agency I need the capability to target anybody and I don’t know until tomorrow who I wish I knew about today, so the easiest solution is to record basically everybody’s web browsing and behaviour and then go from there when I need somebody to look for.

44. Studio shots


COMM

It’s a technology that allows you to rewind time. It can go back years, exposing our each and every search and contact.

That’s a serious threat to everyone’s privacy.

45. Nawal in studio NAWAL PTC

What all this means is that it’s possible
to monitor a country’s entire network of communications. You just need to buy the right kind of high tech solution.

And Evident is one such solution.

46. GV Doha


Nick Weaver set-up/Milipol


COMM

Nick Weaver is a frequent visitor to arms fairs like this one, in Qatar. It keeps him on top of the fast-evolving technology.

Among the conventional arms and war equipment are stalls selling cyber surveillance technologies.

Under international law, this kit is defined as military, since it has the potential for use as an offensive weapon.

Nick is one of the few experts willing to talk openly about mass surveillance.

47.













NICK WEAVER

Every country willing to write a pay cheque to the right party can do this sort of surveillance but no one wants to admit it.

NAWAL
And why is that? Because it’s dangerous?

NICK WEAVER

Because it’s creepy. The notion that all your web surfing is captured… because all that stuff is unencrypted is just frankly creepy. Even if something is never abused, it just disturbs people.

48.
London GVs, computer rack, lights, cables




Theresa May in studio shots

COMM

Creepy or not, there’s little doubt that that mass surveillance can be used to identify criminals and extremists. According to the Home Office, it’s also been significant in every major counter-terrorism investigation of the last decade.

49. Aston

Maj-Gen Jonathan Shaw
Former Head of Cyber Security, UK Ministry of Defence




JONATHAN SHAW SYNC

The more terrorist incidents there are, the more people will start to see the benefits of favouring security over privacy.

And I sense a mood – and that’s all I can do is sense a mood among the public - that has moved the cursor more in favour of security and away from individual privacy, because people recognize it’s a trade-off.

50. NAWAL PTC Parliament

London terrorism attack.

















NAWAL PTC

More than ever, in the wake of the Manchester and London terror attacks, this trade off has been on the mind of the British public and government.

The UK government has a very close relationship with BAE. Last year, the Ministry of Defence spent £4.6bn on BAE equipment, and senior government representatives meet with the company at least once a week.

The UK is considered world expert in cyber intelligence, and BAE has been a major part of that as a key supplier of technical tools to British intelligence agencies.

But the question is should they be selling similar equipment to foreign governments?


BREAK: 15:35

51.
Top Shot Copenhagen, Denmark

Nawal walks into office

COMM

I’ve come back to Denmark, where some new evidence about BAE and its mass surveillance tool has come to light.

52.
Editorial meeting



COMM

I’m meeting reporters from Dagbladet Information, a Danish newspaper.

At the daily editorial meeting, Lasse Skou Andersen is briefing colleagues.

Lasse and Sebastian Gjerding are working with us, investigating the cyber technology made by BAE’s subsidiary in Denmark.

53. Nawal with Lasse looking at UAE FOIs.

Aston

Lasse Skou Anderson
Dagbladet Information
LASSE UPSOT

In all these cases, in the copies that we have of the documents, BAE Systems Applied Intelligence is mentioned as the exporter.

54.
COMM

BAE needs a Danish license to export from its subsidiary here.

Lasse obtained a copy of one of these licenses after making a Freedom of Information Act request to the Danish Business Authority.

BAE was asked if they had any objections. They did, so the DBA blacked out some of the details. Or so they thought.

55.



LASSE SYNC

They tried to redact which company was exporting this stuff to the UAE. And they also tried to redact who was the customer in the UAE. But they messed up their redactions.

So here for instance you can see the end user of the equipment as Ministry of the Interior in the state of UAE. And you can also see which company is selling the system. I’ll just find the place where it’s most visible.

Oh wow. You can see it says BAE Systems Applied Intelligence AS in Norresundby.

That’s incredible.

56.

Graphic COMM

Using the same method of investigation, we’ve established that BAE has sold its Evident technology to Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Morocco and Algeria. The license spells out exactly what it can do.

57. LASSE SYNC

You can see here that what they’re selling is an IP Monitoring and Data analysis system to be used for national security and serious crime investigation.

58. Conventional weapons in studio / graphic




COMM

BAE’s website says the company sells its products according to normal commercial imperatives. It states that the company respects human rights wherever they operate.

In 2016, cyber and intelligence contributed nearly 1.8 billion pounds to company turnover. It’s a lucrative business, but no one at BAE was prepared to discuss it.

BAE Right to Reply

COMM

In a statement the company told us:

‘Our technology plays a crucial role in enabling the UK and its allies to combat the threat of international terrorism. BAE Systems is committed to operating ethically and responsibly. We have robust policies and procedures in place to ensure that our international exports to overseas governments are all fully compliant with international export regulations as well as our own strict criteria to evaluate every potential contract.’

59. Drone shot of Tunis


COMM

So what happens when a country is under surveillance by Evident? I’ve come to Tunisia to find out.

60.
Ben Ali archive and Tunisia Arab Spring


COMM

President Zine el Abidine Ben Ali was Tunisia’s dictator for 23 years before he was overthrown by democratic forces.

He was also an early customer of ETI, the Danish company later bought by BAE.

61.
Into building




COMM

Ben Ali had the Evident system installed in the basement of one of his own houses.
62. Nawal PTC in basement


NAWAL PTC

The temptation for a dictator to control his opposition is great. And more than that, Ben Ali wanted to know what people were thinking too.

63. Basement COMM

Today all that’s left in the basement is one old computer rack.

Tunisian intelligence is a murky world but after weeks of searching, we found someone who operated the Evident system for Ben Ali. His job was to monitor the whole of Tunisia’s internet activity.

An actor portrays him.

64. ‘Mr X’ interview


‘MR X’ SYNC

ETI installed it. Engineers and technicians used to come 5 or 6 days training.

The tool works with keywords. You put in the opponent’s name. You will see all the sites they visit and their blogs and social networks.

65. Nick Weaver interview NICK WEAVER SYNC

An example might be you know these are the people at a protest, that’s your starting point. Or you might know you’re interested in people who have read a given article. And you go from there and build basically a profile of what they do. And then if somebody is really interesting then you can switch to an active attack.

66. Evident graphic sucking data from network. COMM

The information Evident provided about websites, social media, e-mails and blogs was given to a team that worked closely with Ben Ali himself. We found someone from that specialist intelligence unit. His words are spoken by an actor.

67.

‘Mr Y’ interview





‘MR Y’ SYNC

Sometimes they’d ask me to get information about specific people.
I was told to change it or to upload something different

Some information went to the president. Most of it was about his opponents.

68. Mr. X “Aziz” ‘MR X’ SYNC

We focused on all the opposition. There were no exceptions. Ben Ali wanted to know who his friends and his enemies were. He wanted to be told even about sarcasm and jokes.
69.
Prison RECON
COMM

The consequences were no laughing matter for those targeted.

Ben Ali locked up thousands of his opponents. In Tunisia’s prisons torture and illegal killings were commonplace.


70.



‘MR X’

Their families were under constant pressure. I saw their pictures on the internet once they were released, after they’d been tortured or beaten.


AD BREAK TWO

71. Arab Spring archive



COMM

It was in Tunisia in December 2010 that a spark ignited the Arab Spring, events that compelled many governments across the region to seek out state-of-the-art surveillance technologies.

For BAE, this was an opportunity.


72. ETI guilty building shots in studio



COMM

The company approached ETI, the Danish producers of the Evident
surveillance system, and bought it – for 137 million pounds. The deal included long-running contracts with Saudi Arabia.


73.
BAE corporate video

Aston

BAE corporate video COMM

We can reveal that BAE has continued to sell surveillance equipment to Saudi Arabia – as recently as 2016.

74. Top shot

COMM

Inside the country, a well-founded fear of surveillance has led many people to change their behaviour.


75. Aston

Manal al-Sharif
MANAL AL SHARIF SYNC

It used to be “walls have ears”, now it’s “smartphones have ears”. So it’s not easy if you are constantly connected to the internet. You cannot tell if it has switched on your camera or the microphone and are recording everything. It sends them everything and you haven’t a clue.


Manal driving video
COMM

Manal al Sharif is Saudi Arabia’s best-known female activist.

In 2011, inspired by the protests in Tahrir Square, she posted a video promoting her campaign to allow Saudi women to drive.

76.

UPSOT
A woman with a PhD still can’t drive because of the ignorance here.

COMM

She was arrested.

77. Manal interview MANAL AL SHARIF SYNC

When I was released from jail, my manager told me, ‘your phone calls are monitored, your messages are monitored, As well as my messaged my email and my internet at home.’ He told me to be careful.

78.

Manal on computer


COMM

Manal’s campaign was silenced. She believes the Saudi authorities must have hacked her social media.
79.
Aston

James Lynch
Amnesty International












JAMES LYNCH SYNC

The knowledge that there is surveillance being carried out by governments is having a chilling effect.

If you look at a country like Saudi Arabia, where a few years ago there was an emerging human rights community, which was doing some very important work.

Part of that group has left the country for that group has left the country for fear of the consequences of what will happen to them. And the other part of that community is too scared to talk to us because of fear for what they think might happen and they know if they do communicate with us, they’re very likely to be listened to.

80. Setup for Yahya
COMM

I’ve heard about a former Saudi air force officer who also now lives abroad. Yahya Assiri was caught posting pro-democracy statements online. Fearing arrest he had to flee his country.


81.
Aston

Yahya Assiri

YAHYA SYNC

Confidence is low, paranoia has increased. There’s a lot of fear.

I’m not exaggerating if I say that more than 90% of activists in 2011 have now vanished. As the situation in the region changed, so did their beliefs Some were arrested and some were silenced.

82. MANAL SYNC

No country monitors its own people the way they do in the Gulf. They can afford advanced surveillance software.

.

83. Graphic
COMM

Since filming this interview, Manal has moved to Australia.


84. COMM

Like Manal, Yahya felt he had to leave Saudi Arabia. He fears what might happen if people feel they have no freedom of expression.

85. Yahya interview

YAHYA SYNC

With the return of repression young people now see these ideals as impossible dreams. They turn to extremism and violence because those who demanded peaceful change were crushed.

86.
GV Saudi Arabia


COMM

When it comes to human rights, Saudi Arabia is at the bottom of the international league. And as a result, BAE’s arms sales to the Saudis have always been controversial. Some argue it’s actually unlawful for the British government to allow the export of these tools.

87. Aston

Andrew Feinstein
Author, “The Shadow World” ANDREW FEINSTEIN SYNC

If one looks at British arms export law, which covers all sorts of military equipment and training and services, no export license is supposed to be granted if there is a strong chance that the sale of the equipment will increase the likelihood of the breaking of international humanitarian law.

88. COMM

This argument, Andrew Feinstein believes, would also apply to the export of surveillance technology.

89. ANDREW FEINSTEIN SYNC

I have no doubt that the British government is acting illegally in terms of its own laws in selling cyber surveillance equipment to the government of Saudi Arabia.

90. HMG right to reply on allegation of unlawful sales
COMM

We requested interviews with both the Foreign Office and the Department for International Trade, which is responsible for approving exports of cyber equipment. Both declined to speak to us.

91. Top Shot Muscat, Oman






COMM

We have discovered from BAE’s export licenses that the company has also sold its mass surveillance system to Oman. So it’s the next stop in my investigation. It’s long been Britain’s main listening post in the Gulf, and is still an important ally.

I’m here to find out about mass surveillance in action. Because it leaves no trace, it’s almost impossible to know it’s been used. But sometimes, as in Oman, the evidence is strongly suggestive.

Nabhan Al Hanashi’s story begins when he was picked up by the authorities after Oman’s short-lived Arab Spring.

92. Aston

Nabhan al-Hanashi

Footage from Muscat. Coffee shop, treated to look like surveillance. Omani men milling about.

Reconstruction

NABHAN SYNC

It wasn’t an arrest. It was an abduction. Two people abducted me from a coffee shop. I don’t know where they took me. I was kept there for 30 days. It was solitary confinement. Above ground or underground, I didn’t know. I didn’t know where I was. I wasn’t allowed anything.. They’d make it hotter or colder.

93. Archive of protest in 2011


Newspaper clipping
COMM

Nabhan and his friends were calling for the Sultan of Oman’s power to be curbed. That was enough for this paper to brand them as ‘terrorists’. Nabhan was jailed for 18 months.

94. Nabhan iv intercut with archive from 2011 NABHAN SYNC

If I’d carried on, I’d have spent the rest of my life in prison

So I decided to leave Oman

95.
Nabhan in London



COMM

In 2014 Nabhan got asylum in London. People sent him stories of human rights abuse in Oman, so he set up The Omani Human Rights Network to publicise them. All communication with his sources was kept secret.

96.


NABHAN SYNC
The person delivering information doesn’t know the one who verifies it. This is to ensure their safety, and also to maintain confidentiality.
97. Graphics COMM

Despite all Nabhan’s efforts, he believes the information sent to him was being intercepted by the Omani government.

98.
NABHAN SYNC

Some people I was in touch with
were arrested and punished

They were questioned about the information they’d sent me


AD BREAK THREE

99. Nawal walking through backstreets at night

COMM

I wanted to meet one of those arrested in Oman.

We’ll call him Saeed to disguise his identity. An actor speaks his words.

Saeed says the Omani authorities were watching the network members’ private accounts from the outset.

100.
Anonymous interview “Saeed”






‘SAEED’ SYNC


I was in touch with Nabhan and the boys in Britain

No one knew how we communicated

We had an agreement

If I sent something, no one else should know

Even if they were close

COMM

But the precautions were in vain. All those who wrote to Nabhan were picked up by the authorities.

Graphic ‘SAEED’ SYNC


Anyone writing to me was called in

We don’t know how they did it

101.
Reconstruction





COMM

The authorities rounded up 7 members of the network. Nabhan says they were jailed and tortured.

All of them had Nabhan as their common contact.

I’m asking Nick Weaver what this says about the method of surveillance.

102. NICK WEAVER








NICK WEAVER SKYPE SYNC

That probably suggests that they’re doing bulk recording of e-mail metadata.

NAWAL
Bulk recording, do you mean mass surveillance?

NICK WEAVER
Yes, that’s the most suggestive evidence of mass surveillance.

NAWAL
Bulk recording, does that mean mass surveillance?

NICK WEAVER
Yes, that’s the most suggestive evidence of mass surveillance. Once you have a message of interest then it’s a matter of pulling threads. People talk bout surveillance being about looking for needles in haystacks, but it's not. What it is, you have to start with some piece of information.


103. Anonymous Double in vis COMM

Saeed was certain that sooner or later, he’d be arrested.

104.
Graphic map of Oman and UAE.

COMM

He tried to escape from Oman and cross into the UAE. When he arrived at the border crossing, he was detained by the Omani authorities. It’s highly probable he’d been tracked.

105. Anonymous Double in vis


‘SAEED’ SYNC

I was in my brother’s car.
We got to the border

Before I could show my ID,
they asked me to come inside

But the car wasn’t registered in my name

It was my brother’s

106.
Graphic COMM

We don’t know for sure that Evident was the system used to monitor Saeed. But his experience is consistent with what we know about it.

107. NICK WEAVER SKYPE






Detail of page 26 of Evident brochure

NAWAL SYNC
We know that Evident was sold to Oman. Could they have used Evident to do this and is it this powerful?

NICK WEAVER
It certainly seems that way. Page 26 in the brochure.

It’s got cell location viewer, target location, the Investigator package specifically has tools for following phone movements, so it integrates into the phone company’s data and allows you to get the data from the network operator. It really looks like they have that as a selling feature.

108. RECON - Light goes on in dark room. Man being interrogated.

COMM

Saeed was interrogated over 12 days. Even after his release, he believed he was still under surveillance.

109.
SAEED SYNC

I became very cautious.
I was afraid of everyone.

109A. COMM

Saeed feels it’s become too dangerous to report human rights abuses.

109B.

SAEED

The movement is finished

There’s nothing in Oman

It’s abroad now

110. London drone shot

COMM

I’m on my way to a London-based NGO called Privacy international. They investigate government surveillance.

111. Aston

Dr. Gus Hosein,
Privacy International

COMM

Dr. Gus Hosein says that what’s happening in the Arab world is part of a disturbing global trend.

112. Aston
Dr Gus Hosein


GUS HOSEIN SYNC

metadata.Unique Selling Point: The digital age has heralded a new unprecedented means of surveillance, and as more of our personal information goes online, more of our lives are subject to state-sponsored espionage. Governments with dubious human rights records are now using mass surveillance technology to thoroughly track and quell any murmurs of dissent - and it is western companies that are providing the technology to do so. BBC reporter Nawal al-Maghafi investigates
